title: Controversy
hook: in the 1230s some banned and burned his books

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: knowledge leads to kindness. The Guide ends with Jeremiah: mercy, justice, righteousness. Which kindness did you do, and did knowing come first? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

Open a printed Mishneh Torah to a page of its Book of Knowledge and look at the margins. Next to Maimonides' clean Hebrew sit other voices, in smaller type. Some explain him. Some defend him. And a few say, more or less, he's wrong. The book that finished as a pillar of Jewish learning started out as a fight. In his own lifetime people accused him. After his death, some rabbis banned his philosophical writings, and accounts tell of copies being burned. Today's word is that fight, and what came out the other side.
screen: `VOICES IN THE MARGIN.` → `ACCUSED, THEN BANNED.` → `WHAT CAME OUT THE OTHER SIDE.`

segments.voice: Controversy. Turn it four ways. First, the accusation. While Maimonides was alive, some readers said his code barely spoke about the resurrection of the dead, and they wondered whether he believed in it. He answered with a whole essay saying yes, he did, and pointing out that it already stood in his own list of principles. A man known for clarity had to explain himself. Second, the critic in the margin. A scholar in Provence, Rabbi Abraham ben David, known as the Rabad, wrote sharp notes on the code. Where Maimonides calls anyone who imagines God with a body a heretic, the Rabad objects. Greater and better people than that, he writes, held such a view, misled by the plain words of verses. He isn't saying God has a body. He's saying don't call sincere people heretics. Those notes are printed right beside the code. Third, the fire. After Maimonides died, a bitter dispute broke out over his philosophy. Some rabbis feared the Guide and the Book of Knowledge would lead readers away from simple faith, and banned their study. Others defended him just as fiercely. Accounts say his books were burned. Historians still argue over exactly who did what. Fourth, then canon. The rabbis had a phrase for the kind of argument that lasts. An argument for the sake of heaven, says the Mishnah, will endure, like the arguments of Hillel and Shammai. The banned books stayed on the shelf. His principles went into the prayer book. The critic and the criticized now share a page. Controversy did not erase him. It became part of how he is read.
screen: `ACCUSED: DID HE DENY RESURRECTION?` · `THE RABAD'S NOTES IN THE MARGIN.` · `BANNED, AND BURNED.` · `FOR THE SAKE OF HEAVEN, IT ENDURES.` · then, large: `CONTROVERSY, THEN CANON.`

segments.voice: Sit back, and let your breathing even out. Bring to mind a thinker, writer or teacher you have argued with, out loud or in your head. Someone whose ideas made people angry, maybe made you angry. Don't drop the disagreement. Hold it, and next to it, find one thing that person saw clearly. One sentence of credit. Then picture the two of you on a single page, your note in the margin beside their words, both kept. Breathe with that picture. The bell holds the time.
Controversy. In Hebrew, machloket. For Maimonides it meant accusation, critique and even burned books, and then a place at the center of Jewish learning. Today's word.
Your line: controversy, then canon. Today, when you disagree with someone, try saying one thing they got right before you say what they got wrong. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Printed editions of the Mishneh Torah carry commentaries around the text, including the Rabad's critical notes, so disagreement is part of the page students study.

trapdoor: what you thought: a great teacher was honored from the start.
what it means: Maimonides was accused in life, critiqued in the margin, and banned by some after death, then read at the center.
what a scholar hears: the Ma'amar Techiyat HaMetim, the Rabad's hasagot on Teshuvah 3:7, and the Maimonidean controversy, read through Avot 5:17.

notes: The index hook dates the bans and burning to the 1230s; under the claims rule the date is left out of the spoken script. Historians usually place the burning in Paris (or Montpellier) around 1232–1233, and its instigators are debated. Please confirm how much the lesson should say.
'accounts tell of copies being burned' and 'historians still argue over exactly who did what' kept deliberately soft. Please confirm.
Essay on Resurrection: the charge that the Mishneh Torah said little about bodily resurrection, and his answer that he affirmed it (it is his 13th principle). Paraphrased; please confirm.

Rabad's gloss on Teshuvah 3:7 paraphrased ('greater and better than he followed this thought, according to what they saw in verses'). Please confirm wording and that the framing (objecting to the label 'heretic', not affirming corporeality) is fair.
Hook: Rabad's glosses are printed in standard editions of the Mishneh Torah; please confirm they appear on Book of Knowledge pages and soften if needed.
'His principles went into the prayer book' refers to Ani Ma'amin and Yigdal, which are based on the thirteen principles; please confirm phrasing.
